web_evidence.title: Back Roads, a Novel in Progress: A Creative Thesis
web_evidence.note: A University of Delaware master’s thesis annotated bibliography explicitly states that The Prince of Tides uses first-person narrative and flashbacks to follow the Wingo family story.

web_evidence.title: Waves of Memory
web_evidence.note: The Washington Post explicitly identifies Tom Wingo as the first-person narrator of The Prince of Tides while discussing Conroy’s later work with editor Nan Talese.

web_evidence.title: Prince of Tides Summary and Study Guide
web_evidence.note: The whole-book guide states that the narrative is told from protagonist Tom Wingo’s first-person viewpoint and frames his recollections as stories told to Susan Lowenstein.

web_evidence.title: Pat Conroy Writing Styles in The Prince of Tides
web_evidence.note: Its point-of-view analysis says the novel is told through Tom Wingo’s eyes from his earliest life through the ending, with other characters’ stories relayed by Tom.

search_log: Searched “The Prince of Tides Pat Conroy excerpt first chapter narrator Tom Wingo,” “point of view,” “first person,” and “narrated by”; opened the resulting sources before use.

Checked Google Books editions and publisher/library preview routes. Google Books exposed contents and metadata but no readable sustained prose; OverDrive displayed sample controls and descriptions but its prose sample was not fetchable, so neither was used as Tier A person evidence.
Searched the exact phrase “Tom Wingo first-person narrator” and opened the Washington Post, University of Delaware thesis, SuperSummary, BookRags, and eNotes results.

Searched academic and JSTOR material. Understanding Pat Conroy has a dedicated chapter on the novel, but the accessible preview did not expose its point-of-view discussion and was not used as person evidence.

Searched “multiple narrators,” “epistolary,” “alternating point of view,” and “frame narrative.” Results consistently described Tom’s first-person narration framed as recollections told to Susan; no sustained competing base narrator was found.
person_note: Tom Wingo is the controlling participating narrator in both the New York present and the extensive childhood flashbacks. Numerous event quotes independently expose his “I,” “my,” and family-inclusive “we”; third-person-only snippets describe other people from within Tom’s account and therefore remain unmarked rather than establishing a separate third-person strand. Dialogue, gnomic material, paratext, and Savannah’s embedded poem were not promoted to base narration. Academic and credible whole-book web descriptions independently identify Tom’s first-person viewpoint, and targeted searches found no alternating narrator. No authorized sustained online excerpt was readable, but the convergent quote evidence and Tier B/C structural evidence make the remaining uncertainty minor.
